subject: geography
title: Age-Sex Pyramids and Dependency
welcome_lead: Read population pyramids like landscapes — the shape tells you a country's past, present and likely future.
meta_desc: Geography Adventure: age-sex pyramids, dependency ratios and the demographic dividend.
final_note: You have learnt to read a pyramid. Demographics drive economics, politics and policy.

concepts.def: Bar chart showing the proportion of males and females in age cohorts.
Pyramid with a broad base, common in LICs and many MICs with high fertility.
Pyramid with a narrow base and wide upper sections, typical of post-industrial HICs.
Ratio of dependents (under 15 and over 65) to working-age population (15-64).
Economic boost arising when working-age population is large relative to dependents.
Group of individuals born during the same period and ageing together through the pyramid.

walkthroughs.body_html: A wide-based pyramid with rapid narrowing indicates high fertility and high mortality (Niger). A constrictive pyramid with a narrow base indicates low fertility (Japan). 'Stationary' pyramids are roughly rectangular (Sweden). Anomalies — gender imbalances, missing cohorts from war or migration — appear as notches and spikes.

Total dependency ratio sums child and old-age ratios. High child dependency strains education and health systems; high old-age dependency strains pensions and healthcare. Policymakers may respond with extended working lives, immigration or pro-natalist incentives.

When the demographic transition shifts the bulge into working ages — as in much of East Asia from the 1970s — a 'demographic dividend' can boost growth if matched by education, employment and gender equity. India, Indonesia and parts of Africa face similar windows in the coming decades.
